pr_title: NetworkAddressChange.Unix: use async Socket API to wait for events.
pr_body:
By replacing the raw handle with a Socket, we ensure only the handle
we own gets used.

By using the Socket async APIs we no longer need a dedicated Thread
to synchronously read the events.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/64319, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/64441.

cc @ManickaP @wfurt @vdjuric

issue_context.title: NetworkAddressChange.Unix can start reading from unrelated handles.
issue_context.body:
The NetworkAddressChange implementation for Unix has a read loop with a raw handle:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/43ceed5514ca93242ff41f9f1ee53fc108c5dc1b/src/libraries/System.Net.NetworkInformation/src/System/Net/NetworkInformation/NetworkAddressChange.Unix.cs#L173-L179

Between the condition-check in the `while` loop, and passing the handle to `ReadEvents` the handle may be re-used for something other. That means we'll be reading for some one else's file descriptor.

I'll look into fixing this once https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/63963 is merged.

I think we may need to dup() file descriptor to avoid it from getting reassigned unless both original and duplicate fds are closed (we would need to keep track of both).

Alternatively, in a go-lang library `fsnotify`, I [noticed](https://github.com/fsnotify/fsnotify/blob/712fe1d802d8c20c95e843adac4d8b11c1d636d1/inotify.go#L43) that they create additional epoll handle around fd being watched (by inotify) to avoid hitting "fd was reassigned by kernel" race conditions. We are also missing such guards in inotify-based file watcher that maybe the cause of some FileSystemWatcher area issues on Linux.
Triage: It is reliability problem. It is now used in HTTP/3.

review_comments: Is it not possible to create the Socket we need via the Socket's ctor?  If not, what would we need to add to make that possible?  We don't need to block this PR on that if we're missing something, it would just be nice if in the future a separate native function weren't required for this.

It is used to deal with platform specifics:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/4207296a67400056daf4f0f95657fe94aa634d4d/src/native/libs/System.Native/pal_networkchange.c#L29-L41

> It is used to deal with platform specifics:

Understood.  So what would it take to not need that?  A Socket.TryCreate and additional exposed address families?  Additional Bind options?  Etc.  For the next time we or someone else need to do something interesting around socket creation, it'd be nice if it could all be done on top of public surface area.  Again, this isn't to block your PR, but rather to identify gaps we might be able to fill.
Besides the enum values, a `struct sockaddr_nl` `EndPoint` class.
Preexisting your change, but it's a little concerning we're invoking arbitrary user callbacks while holding the s_gate lock.
For good or bad, this causes the events to synchronize with the handler registrations.

By moving this to thread pool we lost ability to test this. Are there any advantages? Is there another way to test this?

I assume we could run out of thread pool threads - or rather consume them faster than new ones can be injected - if there's an error similar to the original one (in this PR or in the future).

> By moving this to thread pool we lost ability to test this.

Can you elaborate?

> I assume we could run out of thread pool threads

Note it's not blocking a thread pool thread.  It's just using one long enough to start the asynchronous operation.

The deleted test checked the process for threads named `".NET Network Address Change"` and made sure there are none after the event callback got unregistered. Since the original problem was that we were leaking them. Now, we don't have any coverage while we redo the logic here. So I'm cautious of reintroducing the same problem we had.

You're right, with `await` in the body we're not blocking any thread. But I guess that instead of threads we'd leak async state machines or rather `SockerAsyncEventArgs` or whatever is used underneath.
